content.description: NATO's July summit will test the alliance's strength and how to secure long-term support for Ukraine. Will there be tension around the table, or a meeting among friends?

content.title: Education Without Pause: How AI and Digitalization Can Strengthen Learning in Times of Crisis
content.description: Pandemics, climate crises, conflicts, and migration have shown that education is one of society’s most vulnerable systems. The question is no longer if children’s learning will be disrupted, but how we ensure that education can continue even when society is under severe pressure.
content.extendedDescription:
AI and digital tools are creating new opportunities to build flexible, resilient educational solutions that improve access to learning, support teachers, and help students continue to grow and develop, even in times of uncertainty. At the same time, this development raises important questions about pedagogy, critical thinking, and how technology can be used to strengthen rather than replace human capability and independent thought.

This seminar explores how Sweden can build the resilient education systems of the future, drawing on both Swedish experiences and lessons from Ukraine, where digitalization and AI are being used to enable continued learning during the ongoing crisis and war. The discussion brings together representatives from business, civil society, and the public sector to examine how education can become a central part of Sweden’s long-term preparedness, innovation capacity, and competitiveness.

content.title: Governance under pressure: data, cloud services and cybersecurity in the public sector
content.description: Cyber threats and geopolitical tensions put pressure on the public sector, while new regulations impose rigorous requirements. How can we protect citizens' data and national security without stopping necessary digital modernisation? The balancing act has never been harder.
content.extendedDescription:
Data is both a strategic asset and a vulnerability. The public sector faces a complex choice: how can we modernise systems and harness cloud services and AI while complying with rapidly changing regulations and facing escalating threats?
This seminar explores the challenge of data governance in an uncertain world. We discuss building operational resilience and ensuring continuity without stalling innovation.
The session addresses:
• Navigating regulation: implementing NIS2, DORA and the AI Act in practice.
• Secure modernisation: strategies for moving to the cloud and using AI without compromising sovereignty and security.
• Cyber resilience: protecting critical infrastructure as the boundary between technology and national security blurs.
Join a discussion on securing Sweden's digital future through proactive data governance.

content.title: How do public agencies and companies ensure joint crisis preparedness in an uncertain world?
content.description: Sweden's preparedness is being tested: the state bears responsibility, but private actors own some of the critical infrastructure. Responding to an uncertain world requires a shift from efficiency-optimised 'Just-in-Time' to security-driven 'Just-in-Case'. How do we work together when the market meets the requirements of total defence?
content.extendedDescription:
In a new normal marked by geopolitical unrest and growing threats to our infrastructure, isolated preparedness plans are no longer enough. Swedish resilience depends on seamless interaction between the public and private sectors. But what does cooperation look like in practice when supply chains are under pressure and national security requirements are weighed against market logic? We bring together leading figures from business's most critical sectors (energy, food, finance and telecoms) and public-agency experts to discuss the way forward for Sweden's total defence.
We discuss:
• From efficiency to robustness: How do we adapt logistics and business models to a 'Just-in-Case' mindset?
• Allocation of responsibility: Where does a company's responsibility end and the state's begin when a crisis strikes?
• Vulnerabilities at the interface: How do we eliminate critical weaknesses between public governance and private operation?
Join a discussion about future crisis preparedness and concrete solutions for a safer Sweden.

content.title: Tomorrow's critical infrastructure – digital preparedness for Sweden and Europe
content.description: Cloud services and AI now underpin the critical infrastructure on which civil defence relies. But who actually controls digital infrastructure, and what happens when geopolitical rules change?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden is currently heavily dependent on a few American cloud providers. This practical choice worked well for a long time but now poses real risks to national security, total defence and freedom of action. The question is no longer whether we need change, but what it should look like and how to achieve it.
The panel discusses concrete steps: how the public sector, defence sector and business can set smarter requirements, build a competitive European cloud sector and combine security with innovation. The goal is not isolation. It is an ecosystem where Europe sets the terms of its own digital future.

content.title: Lebanon – is peace possible?
content.description: The relationship between Israel and Lebanon is an important part of the peace negotiations. Is there a path to genuine peace between Jerusalem and Beirut despite Hezbollah's and Iran's strong position?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's relationship with Israel and the Palestinians has shaped our foreign policy for over seven decades and is one of our most debated issues. But what happened behind closed doors from 1948 to 2026 has never been told. Until now.
In “Från Stockholm till Jerusalem: Den okända historien om Sveriges Mellanösternpolitik”, fifteen Swedish, Israeli and Palestinian prime ministers and foreign ministers, along with around eighty ambassadors and senior politicians, share their experiences and reveal what actually happened behind the scenes.
The book draws on 15 years of research, previously classified archival material and over a hundred in-depth interviews.

content.title: Heta stubben: what role can outdoor recreation play in strengthening Swedish total defence?
content.description: Almost half the population has dangerously poor physical fitness. According to the Defence Commission, public health is highly important to the country's resilience. Are residents total defence's weakest link, and how can organised outdoor recreation strengthen Swedish resilience and preparedness?
content.extendedDescription: Last year's Almedalen success, Heta stubben, is back. With the sea as a backdrop and the aroma of coffee from the camping stove, Friluftsfrämjandet will meet party leaders and other decision-makers on several occasions to discuss their vision for outdoor recreation. Four in five children are not active enough, and almost half of adults have dangerously poor physical fitness. The proportion of children spending time in nature daily has fallen from 78 to 49 per cent in 20 years. Seven in ten Swedes know they are responsible for preparing for a crisis, but only one in three has actually prepared or practised. Each year, Friluftsfrämjandet reaches over 100 000 children and young people through activities that strengthen fitness, navigation, endurance, knowledge and confidence in nature. How does this contribute to total defence, and could guided outdoor recreation play an even bigger role?

content.title: Can circular business models scale up in the fashion industry?
content.description: The fashion industry is producing faster and in greater quantities than ever, while textile waste grows. Can circular business models scale up in an industry built on overproduction?
content.extendedDescription:
The fashion industry is producing more clothing than ever, while textile waste rises rapidly. Fair Action's report Dressed to Waste shows that overproduction is a fundamental problem in an industry whose business models still rely on selling more garments at lower quality and prices.

Although circularity is highlighted as an important solution, many companies lack clear targets to reduce production or increase circular revenue. Meanwhile, fashion accounts for around 10 per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions, underlining the need for transition. The report shows that reducing overproduction and adopting new business models are necessary for real change.

Drawing on Dressed to Waste, the discussion explores circularity, growth and what real transition requires. Researchers, civil society and business representatives discuss circular business models, business value, overproduction and the path towards a fashion industry within planetary boundaries.

content.title: A more brain-aware society and better brain health for children and young people with neurodevelopmental disabilities
content.description: Children and young people with neurodevelopmental disabilities face too many barriers in society. A lack of knowledge about the brain's needs creates inequality, stress and mental ill health. We need a brain-aware society. Research needs to be implemented in practice and in real life to benefit children and young people with neurodevelopmental disabilities.
content.extendedDescription:
More children and young people are receiving neurodevelopmental diagnoses today, while mental ill health, school absence and prolonged stress are increasing. At the same time, we know more than ever about the brain, neurodevelopmental conditions and how environments and social structures affect people's ability to function and feel well.
Yet large parts of society are still built on the idea that people function in roughly the same way.

This open discussion brings together research, lived experience and societal perspectives to explore why so many children, young people and families feel that the systems around them are not working, and what we can actually do about it.

Topics include:
Why neurodevelopmental diagnoses are increasing, mental health and prolonged stress.
School and inclusion, neurodiversity and different ways of functioning.
Early intervention and support, brain capital and the society of the future.

If we build societies that work only for some people, we risk creating unnecessary ill health, exclusion and lost potential for an entire generation.
content.subject: Children/young people

content.title: Why is Sweden choosing unemployment?
content.description: Political leaders have gradually abandoned the goal of full employment. Entirely unnecessarily. The truth is that we can eliminate involuntary unemployment – if we want to. But do politicians really want that?
content.extendedDescription:
Welcome to Almedalen's only real economics seminar!

Drawing on Jakob Segerlind's essay Unnecessary Unemployment, some of Sweden's sharpest minds discuss why Sweden has chosen high unemployment when the USA has repeatedly shown that it does not have to be this way. Instead, we are constrained by pessimistic, outdated calculations of so-called equilibrium unemployment. Unemployment has become a religion.

The focus needs to shift to what actually matters: macroeconomic policy.

Together with a spirited group, that is what we will do from the stage at Donners Eventhall. Come and hear about the policies and solutions that usually become Socialdemokraterna's five years later.
content.subject: Employment/labour market

content.title: Sleepless in the city centre — what tools do municipalities need against reckless driving and traffic disturbances?
content.description: Residents of Swedish cities are affected by nighttime reckless driving, deafening engine noise and aggressive road behaviour, with consequences for safety, the living environment and conditions for business. Municipalities and the police need more tools to tackle recurring traffic disturbances in urban areas.
content.extendedDescription:
Municipalities are already installing noise cameras, introducing nighttime road closures and taking local measures, while the police struggle to prioritise the problem. The technology exists to fine drivers who cause disturbances — but current legislation does not provide sufficient scope.

Meanwhile, other European countries have gone further, and Denmark has introduced stricter rules in recent years, including the possibility of seizing vehicles in cases of serious and disruptive driving.

Swedish municipalities and the police need more tools to tackle recurring traffic disturbances in urban areas. How should safety, privacy and proportionality be balanced? And why is the issue still treated as a local problem when it recurs across the country?

speakerTitles: Head of Local Police Area, Malmö

content.title: Can we meet without titles in a digital, performance-driven society?
content.description: How often do we meet without being defined by what we do? Almedalsveckan is built on encounters. But what happens to our conversations when titles, business cards and phones are left outside? When you cannot introduce yourself by name, profession or employer? When everything else is allowed?
content.extendedDescription:
This is not a seminar. It is not even a networking event — and if it is, it may be Almedalen's least useful one.
It is an experiment in how we meet and what happens when we stop performing and simply exist.

At the door, you encounter a few simple rules:
Put your phone in flight mode, and do not introduce yourself by name, profession or employer. No business cards. No business discussions.

Instead, we open the door to something else.

Inside, conversations without an agenda await. Hosts are present to guide and keep the room alive. Conversation cards with questions and reflections help us move beyond our usual roles towards more human encounters.

What happens when we remove titles and can meet without performance, status or expectations?

This is an experiment in what happens to our conversations — and to ourselves — when we disconnect from the outside world for a while and simply remain present together.

content.title: The gap between gut feeling, research and Nutri-Score — whom should you listen to about eating well?
content.description: Every day, we are inundated with fad diets and alarming reports. At the same time, the food system faces an enormous challenge: we need to eat for both our health and the planet. But why is the gap so wide between what we believe is healthy and what science actually says?
content.extendedDescription:
In this seminar, Erik Lundbom from Verian Group will present findings from a brand-new survey of Swedish attitudes to health and fast food, commissioned by MAX Burgers. The figures reveal a clear conflict between our preferences as customers and the reality on our plates.

In Sweden, Nyckelhålet has been our guide for decades, but it is now being challenged by international systems such as Nutri-Score. What happens when businesses move ahead of public authorities? Can an algorithm guide us correctly, or are we simply creating more confusion? Join a discussion on MAX's roof terrace about bridging the gap between unhealthy cravings and planetary health.

Arrive in good time! Before the seminar, we will offer brand-new burgers and samples of the luxury shake available exclusively during Almedalen.
content.detail: MAX Arena, the restaurant's roof terrace

content.title: Threats to working time – which tasks will go undone?
content.description: Widespread skills shortages, a growing dependency burden and major investment needs. Yet various stakeholders advocate a general reduction in working hours. Which tasks will go undone if we work less?
content.extendedDescription: Despite major challenges from skills shortages, a growing dependency burden and substantial investment needs, various stakeholders advocate a general reduction in working hours in Sweden. Meanwhile, several voices call for removing the qualifying deduction from sick pay, which would significantly increase employers' short-term sickness absence costs and require finding replacements at short notice. At the seminar, you will hear different perspectives on the practical consequences of shorter working hours and removing the deduction. Which tasks risk going undone if we work less?

content.description: In summer 2025, groundwater levels on Gotland were so low that Visby risked being unable to maintain its water supply. content.title: From 130 to 100 litres per person per day – achieving it together
content.description: Water-saving measures in homes are gaining ground. But new technology is not the whole answer. Reducing consumption requires changing our habits and sustaining those changes. How much can be asked of residents? And how do we encourage more tenants to voluntarily reduce their consumption?
content.extendedDescription:
In one year, Gotlandshem's tenants have reduced consumption from 130 to 115 litres per person per day. This is close to Region Gotland's interim target of 112 litres, but still some distance from the long-term target of 100 litres.

What are the limits of what a property owner can achieve alone? How can behaviour be influenced without assigning blame? What is reasonable to ask of a tenant, and what is not?

content.title: Secure access to forest raw materials – a question for Sweden's future
content.description: Sweden's forest industry supplies the world with important everyday products, creates 140,000 jobs across the country and is essential to the green transition. But declining and unpredictable raw material flows risk holding it back.
content.extendedDescription: This is a conversation about the conditions for investment and jobs across the country. How are employment, competitiveness and the climate transition affected when access to forest raw materials becomes increasingly uncertain? What rules need to be established for Sweden to remain a leading industrial nation with a growing bioeconomy? Welcome to a seminar where trade unions, employers and political representatives discuss one of the most crucial issues for our shared future.

content.title: General or targeted government grants: what delivers the greatest benefit for patients and taxpayers?
content.description: The government pays tens of billions in healthcare grants to the regions each year, despite the regions having their own responsibilities and taxation powers. Does the money have the intended effects on care, or does it merely fund deficits? And does it matter whether the grants are general or targeted?
content.extendedDescription:
In 2025, the government paid around SEK 70 billion in healthcare grants, a figure that has doubled since 2015. At the same time, the regions are responsible for healthcare and have their own taxation powers. Are government grants needed at all, and do they lead to real change? The answers depend on whom you ask. SKR argues that general grants give regions scope to set the right priorities and reduce unnecessary administration. During its term, the government has reduced targeted grants and increased general grants, while moving billions from SKR to Socialstyrelsen. Critics argue that the money risks disappearing into regional deficits without measurable effect.
In this seminar, we explore which grant model delivers the greatest benefit for patients and taxpayers.
content.subject: Health and social care

content.title: How can we protect essential services together?
content.description: How do we protect critical infrastructure in an increasingly complex, interconnected society? Examples from Stockholm and Malmö's ports show the importance of responsibility, priorities and collaboration between municipal, regional and national levels in strengthening Sweden's civil defence.
content.extendedDescription: How do we protect critical infrastructure as essential societal functions become increasingly interconnected and interdependent? As operations, ownership and responsibility are divided between municipalities, companies and private actors, complexity and vulnerability increase. The seminar discusses how different levels of society can work together to strengthen protection of strategically important geographical areas and infrastructure. Examples from Stockholm and Malmö's ports raise questions about priorities, the division of responsibilities and how Sweden can develop more robust civil defence amid growing security challenges.

content.title: Resistance to knowledge – what it is, what drives it and how to counter it
content.description: Why do people cling to mistaken beliefs despite strong evidence? Resistance to knowledge is not merely ignorance or a lack of reason, but a complex interaction between psychology, politics and a changing information landscape. What drives it, and what can counter it?
content.extendedDescription: Resistance to knowledge is one of the major societal challenges of our time. Clinging to mistaken beliefs despite strong evidence can have serious consequences, for example weakening trust in democratic institutions, research and media. This can affect everything from willingness to vaccinate and climate engagement to attitudes towards elections. Resistance to knowledge is not simply ignorance or a lack of reason, but a complex interaction between group identity, distrust of established institutions, motivated reasoning and disinformation. But how does it actually work? This discussion starts from new research examining its philosophical, psychological, social and media-related drivers, consequences and remedies, and explores what is needed to counter it. The discussion is part of Vetenskap & Allmänhet's arena for research and democracy.

content.title: How can the EU promote democratisation and human rights when autocratization is the trend?
content.description: As democracy erodes in the EU’s neighbourhood, the effects spill across borders. In Türkiye and Georgia, human rights defenders are pushed back, and elections lose credibility. What does this mean for the EU’s responsibility and ability to act?
content.extendedDescription:
Democracy is sliding backwards in several EU neighbouring countries, which is both a threat to the human rights of the citizens in these countries and creates security concerns for the EU. 
In both Turkiye and Georgia, the human rights situation has deteriorated rapidly in recent years: human rights defenders face considerable repression, and elections in both countries are losing credibility. 
In this session, Kajsa Ollongren, EU Special Representative for Human Rights, will discuss with two prominent human rights defenders from Turkiye and Georgia what the EU can do to promote democratisation when everything is moving in the other direction.

content.title: Material recycling in construction – the key to a circular economy and reduced climate impact
content.description: Construction accounts for large material flows, considerable waste volumes and a substantial share of climate impact. At the same time, a circular economy is crucial both for greater resource efficiency and stronger resilience. What obstacles exist in today's system, and why are materials not circulating to the extent needed?
content.extendedDescription:
Large-scale material recycling can provide a strong foundation for a future circular economy. In practice, however, the market is still characterised by virgin materials often being more competitive than recycled ones.

Why is this, and how can construction genuinely move from waste to resource? What obstacles in today's system hinder circularity? Is progress being slowed by insufficient demand, unclear regulations, difficult permitting processes, business risks or inadequate policy instruments?

This panel brings together politicians, the construction and property sectors, recycling operators and public bodies to discuss how building materials can be recovered in practice. The focus is on concrete solutions throughout the value chain, from procurement and permitting to business models and the allocation of responsibility. What decisions are needed now to strengthen climate benefits, increase resource efficiency and build a more resilient society?

content.title: Growth or staying power – what shapes successful businesses?
content.description: Sweden is one of Europe's best environments for entrepreneurship, characterised by high levels of innovation and technological maturity. But what actually defines a successful business?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden is one of Europe's best environments for entrepreneurship, characterised by high levels of innovation and technological maturity. But what actually defines a successful business?

Entrepreneurship takes many forms. It encompasses everything from tech companies worth billions to solo entrepreneurs, side projects and creators who generate economic value. Success can therefore mean different things: rapid, scalable growth or long-term stability and quality.

In this seminar, we explore the motivations behind entrepreneurship in all its forms. What connects the hobby entrepreneur with the fast-growing tech company?

Together with entrepreneurs, representatives of Fortnox and moderator Per Schlingmann, we discuss what truly builds success. Join a conversation about the many faces of entrepreneurship.

content.title: From skills shortages to competitiveness – how do we secure the future?
content.description: Sweden's technology industry is changing rapidly, with skills determining innovation, growth and global competitiveness. When needs grow faster than the supply of suitable skills, recruitment is not enough. We also need to improve how we educate, attract, develop and retain people.
content.extendedDescription:
At a breakfast panel, Rejlers and Siemens Energy bring together perspectives from Östergötland, a region with strong roots in technology-based industry, rapid growth and increasing skills needs, particularly in STEM. Future jobs exist, but where are the people? Place also matters increasingly: what makes people move here, stay and build their lives here?

Siemens Energy, this year's recipient of Industrins jämställdhetspris, operates in a buoyant international market and needs to recruit 1 000 people over the next few years. With around 600 employees in R&D alone, the question is: how can momentum be maintained?

Rejlers contributes the consulting sector's perspective on developing technical expertise and matching it to industry's needs. Linköpings kommun, Teknikföretagen, Linköpings universitet and Future Place Leadership address business establishments, education, skills provision and what makes people choose a place.

The focus is on moving from skills shortages to long-term competitiveness outside metropolitan regions.

content.title: Can life science investment create growth and resilience? Sweden and Germany as examples
content.description: In a time of growing geopolitical tensions, demographic challenges and strained public finances, investment in innovation is increasingly central to long-term growth and economic stability. Life sciences play a central role but risk losing ground.
content.extendedDescription:
Life sciences, among the most research-intensive and knowledge-driven sectors, play a particularly important role, not only in public health but also in competitiveness, productivity and public finances.

Yet Europe, Germany and Sweden risk losing ground in the global innovation race. Strengthening national and European resilience requires strategic initiatives supporting research, innovation and effective healthcare systems. The Swedish–German innovation partnership offers a unique platform to advance this work and create tangible value for both the economy and society.

Join a breakfast seminar with interactive dialogue, bringing leading political and business representatives and other experts together to discuss how innovation investment can strengthen growth, competitiveness and financial sustainability in Sweden, Germany and Europe.

Breakfast will be served.

content.title: Local politicians' influence and differences in values between politicians and voters
content.description: How much influence do local politicians around the country have, and what differences in values exist between citizens and politicians?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's democracy is based on representative democracy, but how much influence do local representatives have in practice?

This seminar presents findings from Demoskop's recurring survey of Sweden's municipal and regional politicians — Politikerpanelen. How do local politicians perceive their actual influence, how much power do officials in our municipalities and regions have, and can citizens really influence political developments around the country?

Love Edander Arvefjord, consultant at Demoskop and project manager for Politikerpanelen, presents how Sweden's local politicians answer these questions. Johan Martinsson, Head of Public Opinion at Demoskop, then highlights and discusses differences in values between citizens and politicians, and between urban and rural areas. A panel of representatives from politics, the media and research then comments on and discusses the findings.

content.title: Heta stubben: can nature help us find wonder and resilience in a polarised age?
content.description: In a time marked by anxiety, heated debate and widespread mental ill health, many people seek settings that offer calm, meaning and hope. content.extendedDescription:
Last year's Almedalen success, Heta stubben, is back. With the sea as a backdrop and the aroma of coffee from the camping stove, Friluftsfrämjandet will speak on several occasions with senior party figures and other decision-makers about their vision for outdoor recreation. 94 per cent of Swedes believe outdoor recreation is good for health and wellbeing. How can it become as natural a part of societal development as it is of our hearts? How can more people be encouraged to be active in nature?
Four in five children are not active enough, and almost half of adults have dangerously poor fitness. The proportion of children spending time in nature every day has fallen from 80 to 50 per cent over 20 years. While evidence of nature's health benefits has become robust, debate about how we manage forests and nature is often polarised.

content.title: Swedish wool — local processing of a local resource
content.description: Wool is a local raw material that is not fully utilised. Much of the wool shorn annually in Sweden never enters the processing chain. A large-scale wool scouring facility opened on Gotland 10 years ago, followed by a wool spinning mill focused on industry. Has it helped?
content.extendedDescription:
Using the Gotland company Ullkontoret as an example, we describe experiences and opportunities for Swedish wool. Knowledge of wool fibre's beneficial properties, and the fact that so much wool never even reaches the first stage — collection and washing — led us to open a wool scouring facility in 2016. But most of the wool was then sent abroad for further processing. The next step was therefore to establish a spinning mill to supply Swedish industry with large batches of domestic yarn, ready for knitting and weaving machines.

Local processing of local raw materials creates resilience for future challenges, reduces transport needs and thus the CO2 footprint, and provides local jobs. A local wool value chain returns income to the place where wool is produced and strengthens that community. As long as there are sheep, wool will be shorn every year, whether we use it or not.

content.title: Integrated home ownership – the housing option missing from our disadvantaged areas
content.description: How do we tackle segregation in disadvantaged areas and make progress on social sustainability? That is the question society is asking.
content.extendedDescription:
In this panel, we discuss how different forms of housing can contribute to social sustainability, safety and long-term urban development, and which models can help break the happiness paradox. The focus is on how a greater element of home ownership can create more variety in the housing market without sacrificing social stability.

Why is this not done more widely? The panel also examines how increased ownership can strengthen individuals' financial opportunities and engagement in their local area, where people with different incomes and life situations can live side by side.
The discussion focuses not only on social values, but also on documented economic effects and how sustainable housing models can create long-term benefits for property owners, municipalities and society as a whole.

content.title: From exposure to reputation and impact: what do new sponsorship deduction rules mean?
content.description: Sponsorship is undergoing its biggest shift in decades. The government has now submitted a proposal to Lagrådet for tax deductibility of sponsorship as an investment intended to strengthen an organisation's reputation. This will positively affect business, sport, culture and civil society.
content.extendedDescription:
Current rules have largely treated sponsorship as exposure and advertising space. A broader view is now proposed, recognising association, reputation, relationships and long-term value creation. What could this mean for business engagement in sport, culture and social development, and for organisations dependent on these investments?

The seminar explores what this shift could mean for future sponsorship. Drawing on research into association and reputation, lessons from Gyllene Hjulet and SES Effektguide 2.0, we discuss how sponsorship can create greater business and social value, and the effects we actually want to achieve.

Cecilia Perlind from SES Sponsrings & Eventsverige joins Björn Stenvad from Rättighetsbyrån. Panel discussion with Marlene Lindholm, ICA, Camilla Winberg, Head of Partnerships at Friends, and Björn Stenvad.

content.title: Are parents the problem? Vocational programmes and tomorrow's upper secondary schools
content.description: To meet society's skills needs, between 40% and 50% of each age cohort would need to choose a vocational programme at upper secondary school. While young people's interest is growing, a new study suggests their guardians remain resistant.
content.extendedDescription: Several trends also indicate growing interest in vocational education among young people, and one in three upper secondary students has reconsidered their educational choice because of AI. Meanwhile, a new study suggests guardians still prefer their children to choose programmes preparing them for higher education. What should tomorrow's upper secondary schools look like to remain relevant to young people, guardians and society?
content.subject: Education

content.title: From data to decisions in minutes – how AI is changing insight work
content.description: Organisations are drowning in data but are not making better decisions.
content.extendedDescription:
Analysts, communicators and decision-makers face the same paradox: more data than ever, but no greater clarity. Reports pile up, presentations circulate, yet real decisions are delayed. The problem is not access to information. It is the ability to turn it quickly into something that actually changes direction. That is the gap AI is now beginning to close.

The seminar presents how Stella Research Engine is used to turn data into sharp, actionable insights in minutes rather than weeks. The tool changes not only speed but what can actually be delivered.

As a practical example, Svenska kyrkan shares its experiences of working with Ester, the church's own version of Stella. One of Sweden's largest organisations, with responsibilities ranging from parish life to national preparedness, shows how AI support works in practice for communication, strategy and collaboration without requiring technical expertise.
content.subject: Digitalisation

content.title: Is parental insurance equally accessible to all parents?
content.description: Parental insurance is an important tool for promoting gender equality by enabling both women and men to combine family and work. But is it equally accessible to all parents, regardless of background?
content.extendedDescription:
Parental insurance and the right to parental leave are crucial to Sweden's high labour force participation among parents, particularly mothers. At the same time, employment rates differ greatly between groups of parents; for example, foreign-born women have much lower participation than women born in Sweden. How does this relate to differences between groups in the use of parental insurance and leave?

In this discussion, TCO presents a new report examining how the use of parental leave differs between groups according to origin, income and education level. This is followed by a discussion of how to make parental insurance more accessible and ensure that it truly becomes a tool promoting employment and gender equality for all parents, regardless of origin.

content.title: Make gender equality great again?
content.description: Despite many historic advances, progress towards greater gender equality in Sweden has stalled in many areas. Why? And which political reforms are needed to accelerate it?
content.extendedDescription:
Almedalen's major gender equality policy debate! Stress is widespread in female-dominated professions, the gender pay gap remains, the trend towards fathers taking more parental leave has stalled, and women still do more unpaid work at home.

How do we move forward? TCO welcomes you to Almedalen's major gender equality policy debate, with an opening address by author and feminist commentator Emma Holten. This is followed by a political debate between representatives of all parliamentary parties, focusing on two areas crucial to gender equality: parenthood and welfare services. It is when women and men have children that their incomes diverge, and it is primarily women who suffer when welfare services fall short.

The seminar is followed by a gender equality networking reception in TCO-landet.

content.title: Ethics is practice – when technology develops faster than reflection
content.description: Technology is never neutral. AI systems are shaped by people's priorities, blind spots and worldviews. How can we use design to make ethical questions visible and create organisations and decisions where ethics is more than a policy on paper – something actually practised?
content.extendedDescription:
Technology is often developed without a holistic view of how the systems around us affect people socially, organisationally and democratically. What future are we actually building? What do we want to preserve, strengthen or avoid? How do we ensure technological development leads to societies people actually want to live in?

ETHICS IS PRACTICE is a workshop on how AI and digitalisation affect people's judgement, relationships and decisions. We explore why ethics must become part of practice, not just policy documents.

Through reflection, concrete examples and shared exercises using Ethical Impact Canvas, we explore how organisations, designers, decision-makers and the public sector can work more consciously with perspectives, inclusion and human consequences when developing technology and services.

The aim is not consensus. It is to create a safe space for new perspectives, inspiration and practical knowledge.

Please note that Tornrummet is very small and holds only 20 people.

content.title: Put jobs first: skills supply in a new era
content.description: The climate transition, digitalisation, AI development and an ageing population place new demands on labour market and education policy. Meanwhile, unemployment is high. How do we meet society's skills needs in these times? What must politics deliver in the next electoral term?
content.extendedDescription: Despite visions and discussions, governments of different political colours have failed on labour market policy: unemployment is higher than necessary, and many unemployed people do not receive the right support or have been out of work for a long time. Conditions for matching people to jobs are therefore harder than they have been for many years. TCO's skills supply policy programme and this labour market debate start from the need to move from words to action. What concrete changes are needed to reduce unemployment and increase employment, thereby strengthening the long-term skills supply? With researchers and political representatives, we seek to answer how putting jobs first can solve skills supply challenges.

content.title: Sweden needs every last person – is migration policy getting in the way?
content.description: Sweden needs more people in work to secure its supply of skills. How can migration contribute to a stronger labour market? If Sweden needs every last person, how can policy make that possible?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden faces a growing dilemma: while labour shortages are severe in both welfare services and business, it has become harder for people who already work and contribute to stay. Immigrant workers are now essential to a functioning labour market, yet regulations are tightening and uncertainty is increasing.
What would migration to Sweden that strengthens the labour market look like? How can we avoid wasting skills through complicated permit procedures, insecure conditions and signals that reduce people's willingness and ability to work in Sweden? And how can we combine order and predictability with a policy that makes use of people's willingness and ability to contribute? The seminar opens with a conversation between representatives of academia and business about how current policy affects the labour market. We then speak with political representatives about their responsibilities and proposals.

content.title: Research espionage in the Nordic region – how can we protect innovation without slowing it down?
content.description: Research, technology and dual-use capabilities are strategic assets. In a heightened security situation, they must develop quickly and securely. As the EU, Sweden and the Nordic region strengthen research security, the question grows: how can we protect research from espionage without inhibiting openness, collaboration and growth?
content.extendedDescription:
Research espionage, espionage and research security have become increasingly important issues for universities, science parks, startups, investors and research-intensive companies. New technology, research data, international partnerships and dual-use capabilities can now have commercial, strategic and security-policy significance.

The EU and Sweden are strengthening work on research security, responsible internationalisation and secure innovation processes. Meanwhile, Nordic cooperation in defence, preparedness, industry and technology is deepening, including through NATO and joint Nordic initiatives.

The question is no longer whether research security is needed, but how to introduce it without unnecessary friction. When numerous collaborations, people and access rights need managing, isolated measures are insufficient. Scalable, proportionate and documented methods are needed, such as risk assessments, role analyses and background checks where relevant and permitted.
content.subject: Security/defence

content.title: How to achieve a nature-positive energy transition
content.description: How can solar parks on agricultural and forest land become nature-positive? Where is solar farming most suitable, how should parks be designed, and what regulations are needed for large-scale solar energy to enhance biodiversity and help meet the EU Nature Restoration Law?
content.extendedDescription:
This panel discussion explores how solar parks on agricultural and forest land can become a practical tool for a nature-positive energy transition. The starting point is that solar farming, when properly located and designed, can enhance biodiversity, create new meadow and wetland habitats and help meet the EU Nature Restoration Law. The discussion examines three areas:

1. Site selection: How do we find locations where solar farming can best coexist with agriculture and forestry while creating new or enhanced ecological value?

2. Design: How can solar parks — including their management, layout and surroundings — be designed to deliver clear benefits for biodiversity and nature restoration?

3. Policy instruments and the EU Nature Restoration Law: How can legislation and policy instruments help steer development towards nature-positive solutions, and what roles do public authorities, businesses and civil society play?

content.title: More generations at work — but are workplaces ready?
content.description: Our labour market has five working generations and a rapidly growing proportion of older workers. More people are pursuing further education and changing careers later in life. This places new demands on how workplaces are designed, operate and are led.

content.title: Cosmic — what happened and what does the future hold?
content.description: The rollout of the Cosmic electronic health record system in many regions has sparked considerable debate. On one hand, technical problems, poor coordination and risks to patient safety; on the other, the need for a shared health record system to improve information sharing and collaboration in healthcare. What happens now?
content.extendedDescription:
The rollout of the Cosmic electronic health record system in many regions has sparked considerable debate and criticism. Many describe it as an integration failure. Technical problems and poor coordination between steering groups and users led to frustration and inefficiency in hospitals. There have been warnings that patient safety has been jeopardised, and critics argue that the rollout should have been halted.

At the same time, some view Cosmic as a long-term investment. A shared health record system can improve information sharing, patient safety and collaboration in healthcare. The question is therefore not only what went wrong, but also what the future should look like. Is better training, more testing and greater influence for healthcare staff needed? We will hear views from users, the supplier and researchers.

content.title: Is the EU changing innovation funding, and how will Sweden be affected?
content.description: The EU's next cohesion policy programming period may change how innovation is funded, with signs of increased national control. What does this mean for those building innovation across the country, and how is Sweden influencing developments?
content.extendedDescription:
The EU's next cohesion policy programming period is taking shape, with proposals that could change funding for innovation and regional development. New governance models are being discussed in which national priorities may carry more weight than before.

For actors working closely with businesses and innovation across the country, this could change conditions for funding, influence and working methods.

Meanwhile, negotiations are under way in which member states and other stakeholders can influence developments. But how is Sweden positioning itself? Which perspectives are we promoting, and which risk having less impact?

This seminar brings together decision-makers and actors from different parts of the system to discuss what we know about EU-level developments, what they may mean in practice and what is needed to adapt and exert influence in time.

A networking lunch is served from 1200, with limited places. The seminar starts at 1230.

content.title: Education in the AI era – what role does a university actually have now?
content.description: When knowledge is freely available online and AI can answer almost any question, anywhere and at any time, what role do universities have? How are society's expectations of higher education institutions changing in the AI era, and how do universities themselves view their mission?
content.extendedDescription:
Rapid developments in AI are changing how we seek information, learn new things and make decisions. At the same time, the technology raises questions about universities' role in the society of the future. What should students, employers, public authorities and other stakeholders be able to expect from universities in the AI era? If AI can summarise research, write texts and provide sophisticated answers in seconds, what becomes the universities' role?

The discussion examines how universities are affected by AI developments, as well as the responsibility of higher education institutions in a society where the boundary between knowledge, information and automated answers is increasingly blurred. Which human capabilities become important when technology can do more and more?

content.title: How can Sweden's textile industry grow?
content.description: Sweden has the potential to become a world leader in sustainable textile development, circular flows and future production. How do we accelerate progress?
content.extendedDescription: Sweden is a textile nation of global significance. The sector is among the country's most employment-intensive industries, driving jobs, regional development and economic stability. But this is only the beginning. Sweden has the potential to lead the world in sustainable textile development, circular flows and future production. Unlocking that potential requires a national effort. Textile Valley is the hub of this movement, a unique creative ecosystem connecting education, research, entrepreneurship, design, production and commerce. At its heart is Högskolan i Borås, already offering one of the world's leading textile education programmes, with research and testing environments unparalleled in the Nordic region. The next step is logical: Sweden needs a textile university to strengthen national textile expertise and research, attract international talent and educate the workforce needed for the industry to grow nationwide.

content.title: No driving licence, no job? The gap holding back Sweden's labour market
content.description: Driving licence requirements exclude young people from the labour market, while healthcare, social care and skilled trades are crying out for workers. How can we lower the barriers?
content.extendedDescription:
Unemployment, particularly among young people, is one of Sweden's major societal challenges. At the same time, several sectors face substantial recruitment needs.

Public debate often focuses on education, integration and labour market matching, but less often on the role of a driving licence. For many young people, having a driving licence has effectively become a decisive barrier to entering employment.

Sweden has one of Europe's highest rates of youth unemployment, and more than 126 000 young adults are currently out of work. Meanwhile, demand for workers is high in healthcare, services and skilled trades, where a driving licence is often a basic requirement. But young people do not have equal opportunities to obtain one. This creates a gap in the labour market: employers struggle to recruit, while many young people are excluded before they have even had a chance.

How can we lower the barriers and improve employers' access to skills? The seminar draws on current data and young people's own experiences of how a driving licence affects their chances of getting a job.

content.title: Sweden creates world-class deep tech – so why are companies leaving?
content.description: Sweden ranks among the world's leaders in research, patents and deep tech startups per capita. Yet too many of our most promising companies scale or seek capital abroad, or are acquired by foreign giants. Why do they not stay, and what can we do about it?

content.title: Environmental Product Declarations for construction products: From nice to have to must have
content.description: Environmental Product Declarations (EPDs) for construction products have become increasingly prominent. With the entry into force of the revised EU Construction Products Regulation (CPR-2024), it will become mandatory for certain products to provide information on environmental impact indicators.
content.extendedDescription:
An EPD is a document that contains objective, comparable information, verified by a third party, on the environmental performance of products and services. The relevant European standard, EN 15804:2012+A2:2019, determines 13 mandatory core environmental impact indicators, with the option to include 6 additional reporting categories related to human health and land use.

In the construction sector, EPD are used to provide information on products and services, facilitating a Whole-Building Life Cycle Assessment (WBLCA).

The EU Construction Products Regulation published in 2024 (CPR-2024), regulates that for construction products for which a harmonised technical specification exists (usually a harmonised EN standard), certain environmental impact indicators must be provided. This obligation will be introduced in steps, starting with the Global Warming Potential (GWP).

This topic will be covered in a lecture supported by slides, followed by a question-and-answer session.
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: AI is a climate blind spot: how do we make emissions visible?
content.description: AI is advancing at remarkable speed, but also increasing energy consumption and emissions. Yet established methods for calculating its climate impact are lacking and transparency is low. How can companies take responsibility for emissions they cannot measure?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden has just launched its first AI strategy, aiming to rank among the world's top 10. AI use is growing explosively, along with energy consumption and carbon dioxide emissions. Companies seeking an accurate picture of their climate impact increasingly need to calculate AI emissions. The problem is a lack of methodology and accessible data, making calculation difficult.
2050 Consulting and Klimatkollen have developed an initial methodology and a simplified, free calculator for companies to estimate emissions from their AI use. The calculator launches at this seminar, which invites small and large AI companies, politicians, finance and business representatives to discuss AI's impact, transparency in climate data and measuring something changing rapidly.

content.title: How can Mälardalen and Sweden win the competition for skills?
content.description: Swedish employers lack around 61,000 people with the right skills. Three in four say recruitment is difficult, and one in four recruitment attempts fails. Meanwhile, many highly educated people are unemployed or work below their skill level. These are not coincidences – they are a systemic failure.
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden attracts international talent, but lengthy establishment processes and inadequate integration mean we lose it again. Swedish higher education institutions attract international students, but only one in four remains in the Swedish labour market after graduation, although three in four want to.

Stockholm-Mälardalen has Sweden's largest labour market and its strongest concentration of industry, energy systems, logistics and technology-intensive companies. Skills shortages have immediate consequences here: investments are delayed, expansion fails to materialise and the transition slows.

content.title: From linear to circular thinking – who takes the risk as the construction sector transitions?
content.description: Sweden aims to reach net-zero emissions by 2045. But business conditions in construction and real estate are already changing rapidly in the run-up to 2030. Does the construction industry risk using the wrong calculations for 2030 and underestimating how quickly climate requirements are becoming business-critical?
content.extendedDescription:
The construction and real estate sector currently accounts for around 20 per cent of Sweden's total greenhouse gas emissions. A large share arises during construction and materials production, in the manufacture of cement, steel and other building materials.

Circular materials and solutions already exist and can substantially reduce climate impact. At the same time, the industry is characterised by complex value chains in which standards, procurement and risk models are still designed around a linear business model.

Does the construction industry risk using the wrong calculations for 2030 and underestimating how quickly climate requirements are becoming business-critical? This panel brings together industry, construction and real estate to discuss how costs, risk and incentives need to be distributed across the value chain to make net zero possible in

content.title: What reforms does Sweden need to improve life for people with rare diseases?
content.description: To strengthen care for people with rare diseases, Sweden must cooperate on diagnostics, care pathways, coordination between national and regional levels, skills supply, research and follow-up of actual treatment outcomes.
content.extendedDescription:
Work to strengthen care for people with rare diseases has made important progress in recent years. Political engagement has grown, national inquiries have been commissioned and several authorities have been tasked with improving access to care, treatment and follow-up. Yet major challenges remain. The path from innovation to actual patient benefit is often long, unequal and difficult to navigate. For patients with rare diseases, this can mean delayed diagnosis, differing care between regions and long waits for innovative treatments.

What reforms are needed? What do the parties want to see in 2026? How can responsibility, incentives and cooperation evolve to improve access to new rare-disease treatments in Sweden?

content.title: Digital sovereignty and digital dependence – building total defence in a digitalised society
content.description: Sweden is one of the world's most digitalised countries, but also depends on global technologies and cloud services. How are our security, robustness and freedom of action affected by cyberattacks or disruptions?
content.extendedDescription:
How can we build robust total defence in a society heavily dependent on digital infrastructure, global cloud services and strategic technologies such as AI? Sweden is one of the world's most digitalised countries, but digitalisation also creates new vulnerabilities. Cyberattacks, information influence operations and dependence on foreign platforms raise questions about cybersecurity, digital sovereignty and national freedom of action.

The seminar examines how data, AI and other strategic technologies affect future total defence and what skills, research environments and technical capabilities Sweden needs to develop to strengthen society's resilience. It also addresses collaboration between the public sector, business and academia to build secure digital systems, reduce strategic dependencies and strengthen Sweden's ability to act in an uncertain, rapidly changing world. Innovation, research and skills supply for future security are also in focus.

content.title: How do we strengthen medicine preparedness throughout Sweden?
content.description: When medicines are unavailable or need to be redistributed, questions arise in everyday healthcare: How do we strengthen regions' ability to prevent and manage shortages? And what national coordination is needed to meet regional challenges?
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar starts from the government's assignment to Läkemedelsverket and Försvarsmakten to analyse how medicines are managed and distributed within Försvarsmakten and in cooperation with other organisations, to enable more appropriate medicine management and better cooperation between civilian and military healthcare.

Alongside this assignment, broader national efforts are under way to secure access to medicines. The inquiry Säkrare tillgång till läkemedel will, among other things, propose measures to prevent and manage supply disruptions and shortages, including antibiotics, review a national coordination and purchasing function, and analyse how the allocation and redistribution of medicines can work better. The government and SKR have also reached an agreement for 2026 on stronger stockholding ahead of new requirements for regions from 2027.

content.title: Research and infrastructure for security in northern Sweden
content.description: Northern Sweden is gaining strategic importance for energy, raw materials and security. This requires strong total defence, with research, innovation and skills strengthening societal resilience. The region's unique environments also make it an important testbed for new technology.
content.extendedDescription:
Northern Sweden has growing strategic importance for energy, raw materials, the climate transition and security. This places greater demands on robust total defence, with knowledge, innovation and societal resilience as important components.

Research helps us understand and address complex threats, from cyberattacks to supply-chain disruptions. Research infrastructure also serves as test environments where new solutions can be developed and tested under realistic conditions. Northern Sweden's unique circumstances make the region an important testbed.

Universities play a central role by educating skilled people, conducting relevant research and fostering collaboration between academia, business and public actors. Investment in research and infrastructure therefore strengthens not just the region, but Sweden's total defence and resilience as a whole. The seminar examines how these elements can develop together.

content.title: From tithes to a billionaire tax – taxation according to ability to pay, then, now and in the future
content.description: For most of history, tax has been about morality, justice and building society rather than marginal effects and incentives. Who should contribute, how much, and to what?
content.extendedDescription:
From tithes paid to the church to today's discussions of a billionaire tax, attitudes to taxation have reflected society's ideas about justice, responsibility and community.

content.title: When will the energy grid be flexible enough to avoid new construction – and what will it take to get there?
content.description: Sweden is expanding renewable electricity generation at a record pace. At the same time, pressure is growing from data centres, new industry and electrified transport, all competing for the same renewable kilowatt-hours. How do we make it all work together?
content.extendedDescription:
The technology for flexibility, energy storage and demand management exists, but we are still not making the leap from individual systems to large-scale solutions. The connection queue is growing, regulations were designed for an electricity system that no longer exists, and despite long-standing discussions about a national energy digitalisation plan, no one has taken overall responsibility for digitalising the grid and providing the digital connections that should hold the whole system together.
This panel discusses what is needed for flexible energy management to move from isolated success stories to a broad system-wide solution for Swedish industry: which business models and regulations need to change, how risks should be shared, and who will lead digitalisation.

content.title: Jobs that did not exist three years ago – how do we solve industry's skills shortage?
content.description: Sweden has one of Europe's strongest technology industries and innovation capabilities, but also one of its most serious skills shortages. Industry is crying out for engineers while AI and automation change the skills actually needed. How do we solve industry's skills shortage?
content.extendedDescription:
Six in ten industrial companies say finding the right skills has become harder. Demand is greatest for roles such as industrial electricians, toolmakers and automation technicians, but Swedish industry needs to recruit more than 230,000 people in total within three years. The education system cannot keep up, the pace of transition is uneven and international recruitment is politically sensitive but commercially unavoidable.

Companies that fail to secure skills lose ground. Yet some initiatives work: reskilling programmes, academia–industry collaborations and new routes into technical professions.
Who takes responsibility: companies, the state or academia? Which models can scale? And how do we ensure the transition does not leave parts of the workforce behind?

content.title: Robots that see, act and decide – what does Sweden need to lead the next industrial wave?
content.description: Sweden has world-leading industrial companies, strong research environments and a growing robotics and AI ecosystem. But technology has outpaced governance, and industry, politicians and investors must now come together. How do we create tomorrow's manufacturing industry?
content.extendedDescription:
What is changing Swedish industry now is not a chat interface: it is robots trained in simulations, deployed in production and making decisions without a human in the loop. Autonomous systems are taking over assembly lines, logistics flows and process industries, and Sweden is in the midst of this transformation.

Yet too many initiatives remain stuck in the pilot phase. Skills are unevenly distributed. Test environments, partnerships and capital are insufficient, and questions of data, responsibility and business value in human–machine systems remain far from resolved. Who owns decisions when machines make them?

Physical AI is changing industrial production faster than policymakers can respond. Sweden risks falling behind. What is required of policy, technology and leadership for the Swedish industrial model to survive this shift and take the lead ahead of countries now automating at record speed? What does leadership require when physical AI sets a new standard?

content.title: The local energy transition – how should we build, own and finance it?
content.description: Sweden needs to expand electricity grids, local energy production, flexibility and digital infrastructure at a pace no single stakeholder can achieve alone. What needs to change to make the local energy transition investable on a larger scale, and what role can politicians play in creating long-term ground rules?
content.extendedDescription:
Municipalities are close to local needs but cannot bear all the investment risk. Capital markets seek long-term sustainable assets but often lack local roots and the capacity to deliver. Locally rooted energy companies, meanwhile, rarely have access to the capital the transition requires.

The gap between local public benefit and investment capacity remains large. Business models and ownership structures were built for a different energy system. And the question of who should take overall responsibility for local infrastructure, including electricity grids, fibre, district heating and local production, is far from resolved.

This panel discusses how municipalities, investors and locally rooted energy companies can build the infrastructure of the future together. What new partnerships and ownership models are needed? How should risk and return be shared? What needs to change to make the local energy transition investable on a larger scale, and what role can politicians play?

content.title: From flexibility to storage – does energy need a new financing model?
content.description: Sweden is rapidly expanding electricity generation to meet its 2045 climate and energy targets. Demand for flexibility and battery storage is also growing: solutions that ease and stabilise the grid, smooth peaks in power demand and make renewable energy available when needed. But how will it all be paid for?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden is rapidly expanding electricity generation to meet its 2045 climate and energy targets. Demand for flexibility and battery storage is also growing: solutions that ease and stabilise the grid, smooth peaks in power demand and make renewable energy available when needed.

Scaling up requires capital. But many investors and lenders remain more familiar with traditional energy assets. Flexibility and storage often involve multiple revenue streams, new contracts and a rapidly evolving market, demanding new approaches to assessing, pricing and packaging risk.

This panel discusses unlocking more capital for energy storage and flexibility. Are new financing and contractual models needed to make more projects investable? How should risk be shared? What incentives are needed, and what role can politicians play in creating long-term ground rules? Are there international examples to learn from?

content.title: With billions at stake — what leadership does the energy transition require?
content.description: The energy transition is the biggest societal project of our time, with billions at stake. What leadership is needed to bring it to fruition — in business, politics and the energy sector?
content.extendedDescription:
The climate crisis, geopolitical uncertainty and an energy system undergoing major change are forcing businesses and societies to make major, crucial decisions in a short time.

The leadership required must navigate uncertainty and investments, manage risks and drive through changes in a system that has traditionally moved slowly. At the same time, newcomers in new energy are challenging established practices in a sector where investments have long been long-term and the pace of change slow.

How do you lead in a sector where the pace is accelerating rapidly, reality is complex and decisions will shape the energy system, businesses and people's everyday lives for decades to come?

This panel brings together entrepreneurs, industry leaders, investors and decision-makers to discuss the leadership needed as the energy system is reshaped, and what determines who wins and loses in the energy transition.

content.title: Sweden is building resilience at record speed — could outdated thinking hold everything back?
content.description: The largest military expansion of modern times is under way, driven by the need to strengthen not only Sweden's defence capability but the resilience of society as a whole. But are we stuck in an old system?
content.extendedDescription:
The largest military expansion of modern times is under way, but the models for purchasing and building capability are not keeping pace. Investment in defence properties is expected to increase by 100 per cent within a few years, while procurement systems remain based on detailed management and control, designed for a stable world that no longer exists.

The research is clear: when pace and uncertainty increase, traditional client–supplier relationships inhibit innovation and erode trust. LUFS and LOU often allow more room than is used — the question is whether we dare to use it.

This panel brings together public-sector clients, industry and legal expertise to discuss building strategic partnerships within existing rules and what is needed to prevent outdated thinking from holding back a historic transition.

content.title: When premises stand empty – who dares untangle the VAT problem?
content.description: Premises exist. Demand is enormous. Yet supply does not meet demand. Why? Across Sweden, sports clubs must turn away children and young people because they cannot access premises. Meanwhile, premises stand empty or are rented to others. Why? The answer is VAT.
content.extendedDescription:
Today's VAT rules make it uncertain and sometimes unprofitable for property owners to rent to organisations not conducting VAT-liable activities on the premises. The result is a system that excludes sport, culture and other parts of civil society from the premises market, despite considerable need and obvious public benefit.

For many sports clubs, finding premises has become a constant obstacle to developing their activities and, at worst, a threat to their existence. How do the rules affect property owners' ability to rent out premises, and what trade-offs are actually made in practice?

Can we create a system where anyone can rent any kind of premises, regardless of VAT status? A government inquiry argues that changes risk increasing costs. Others argue that doing nothing is considerably more expensive, through lost activities, limited growth and weaker civil society. So what is the real problem, and what will it take to solve it?

content.title: Can the economy grow within planetary boundaries – and which companies can turn this into a competitive advantage?
content.description: The research is clear: humanity has already exceeded several planetary boundaries, while global production and consumption continue to increase. So can the economy continue to grow within planetary boundaries, and if so, how?
content.extendedDescription:
The research is clear: humanity has already exceeded several planetary boundaries, while global production and consumption continue to increase. For businesses, this means a new reality in which climate, resource use and biodiversity are no longer merely sustainability issues, but direct business risks as well as new competitive advantages.

At the same time, a new business logic is emerging: studies show that companies integrating climate data, resource efficiency and governance into their core operations perform better over time, are more resilient in crises, attract capital more easily and identify new business opportunities in the transition.

Yet most companies remain in a linear business model that depletes the planet.

This panel brings together entrepreneurs, investors and business leaders to discuss how growth, capital and climate responsibility can be combined in practice, and why companies that start measuring and managing their impact also become the winners of the future.

content.title: How do we enable constructive dialogue on the environment and sustainability?
content.description: Challenges such as the energy transition and the climate crisis require constructive dialogue to resolve. Yet trust in research is faltering, facts are questioned and polarising narratives clash. How can we work together to achieve constructive discussions and communication methods that work in practice?
content.extendedDescription:
Environmental and climate crises are accompanied by disagreements, polarising conflicts and unproductive dialogue. When these crises intensify public debate, it becomes harder to create constructive discussions that lead to practical solutions.

In a co-creative panel discussion, researchers and communicators invite a conversation about how we can navigate these disagreements and create conditions for different perspectives to meet. How can democratic dialogue and participation be strengthened on issues relating to climate and energy? How can discussions about the environment and sustainability contribute to progress rather than polarising conflicts?

The panel discussion exchanges ideas about dialogue-based environmental communication, drawing on visitors', researchers' and communicators' own experiences. Together, we discuss how environmental and sustainability issues are discussed during and outside Almedalsveckan, and how those discussions could take place.

The panel discussion is organised by the Mistra Environmental Communication research programme.

content.title: What is happening to our quality registers?
content.description: Sweden's quality registers are a unique resource for healthcare research, development and improvement, but what happens now that the funding model is changing?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's quality registers are a unique resource for healthcare research, development and improvement. But their new funding model has sparked debate. Researchers and doctors worry that higher requirements for regional co-funding and demonstrable results could threaten the registers' future. They also warn of poorer data quality and a weakening of Sweden's international position in medical research.

Supporters of the new model believe the registers must be used more efficiently and demonstrate greater benefits for healthcare. Both sides meet on Läkartidningen's stage for a topical and engaging discussion.

content.title: How can home savings and sustainable construction help more young people get a home of their own?
content.description: How can more people have the opportunity to save for their own home while construction becomes more sustainable and climate impact decreases?
content.extendedDescription: Saving for a home has long been central to home ownership and an important foundation for social stability and financial security. Yet Sweden faces major challenges involving high barriers to entering the housing market, rising construction costs and stricter climate requirements. This discussion brings together housing policy, finance, construction and community development stakeholders to explore how new ideas about home savings can create more routes into the housing market. It focuses on connecting savings, long-term thinking and sustainable investment more closely with future housing construction, at a time when rising CO₂ costs also affect the economy. TRIQBRIQ organises the seminar to create an open meeting place for new thinking on home savings, ownership and future sustainable societal models in Sweden and the Nordic region. The discussion starts from the need for solutions that improve young people's ability to save for housing while stimulating sustainable construction and lasting responsibility.

content.description: According to the government's AI strategy, Sweden aims to become the world leader in AI in public administration. So how can public agencies use AI to develop their operations without compromising legal certainty, quality and public trust?

content.title: What is quantum, really – and why is everyone talking about it?
content.description: Quantum physics describes how the universe's smallest building blocks work. Ordinary physical laws are not enough there, and probabilities govern. But what does that mean in practice – and how does it differ from classical physics?
content.extendedDescription:
Join a journey into a world where reality behaves differently from what we are used to, and where the technology of the future is taking shape.

In this conversation, we explore what quantum is and how it is applied today. We also discuss how we know quantum works, why quantum technology could be crucial to the future, and whether you can really be in two places at once.

Welcome to a conversation with quantum professor Peter Samuelsson, who works in Lunds universitet's Nobel Prize-winning research environment.
