content.title: Stable growth on three pillars – what is sustainable urban development in 2026?
content.description: Growing cities bring both opportunities and challenges. How can growth, social sustainability and the climate transition be combined in practice?
content.extendedDescription:
Norrköping and Malmö are developing at a rapid pace. Populations are growing, neighbourhoods are being transformed and demands for climate-smart, socially sustainable development are increasing. But how do we create stable growth that lasts economically, socially and environmentally?

Major urban transformation is under way in Norrköping, while Malmö focuses on social sustainability and climate-smart urban development. Exclusion, safety and future urban environments are high on both cities' agendas.

Meanwhile, energy systems, coordinated planning and business investment are crucial to a just transition. How can partnerships between municipalities, business and academia contribute to attractive, inclusive cities?

Join a discussion bringing together political leaders, business and experts to explore what sustainable urban development means in practice and how we can build stable growth on three pillars together.

content.title: Organised crime in Swedish sport
content.description: What do we know about organised crime's impact on Swedish sport, and what capacity exists to detect, prevent and address it? What can be done to reverse the trend, and what role do sport, the police and others have in this work?
content.extendedDescription: A new report produced by Stiftelsen Tryggare Sverige on behalf of Riksidrottsförbundet shows that organised crime in Swedish sport is widespread and affects both elite and grassroots clubs, large and small. This particularly concerns criminal infiltration and, to some extent, the recruitment of children and young people into criminal gangs. Nor are the problems confined to football or disadvantaged areas, as public debate can easily suggest. What do we know about organised crime's impact on Swedish sport, and what capacity exists to detect, prevent and address it? What can be done to reverse the trend, and what role do sport, the police and others have in this work?

content.description: An attractive city never stands still. It grows to meet the needs of residents and other stakeholders. What makes a city relevant to residents, businesses, talent and visitors? content.extendedDescription: How can we find new ways of working that draw on residents' energy in urban development over the long term? As cities grow, new opportunities emerge to improve accessibility and develop lively meeting places and attractive living environments. content.title: The journey to energy class A: turning costs into value-creating investments
content.description: Energy efficiency and sustainability are no longer future issues. New regulations change the playing field for property owners and demand investment, cooperation and new working methods. How can the journey towards better energy ratings be profitable?
content.extendedDescription:
Energy efficiency, sustainability and a smaller climate footprint are not just buzzwords. Regulations are arriving rapidly, increasing demands on property owners and changing the playing field. Large investments, conflicting objectives and communication problems can undermine profitability. Technology, sustainability and economics play different roles in a profitable journey towards a better energy rating. New thinking, perspectives and actors are required.

A building is designed to last around 100 years. Conditions are now changing rapidly: the green transition, rising energy prices and global instability with various threats. Building anew is not an option. How do we develop existing properties? Securing operations and finances requires new approaches, funding and skills. Several actors have made considerable progress and have solutions. How do they think, what have they done, and what results and lessons have emerged? Solutions are created together.

content.title: Who represents voters in nicotine policy?
content.description: Who represents voters as the EU tightens its grip on nicotine policy? Two new surveys show how Swedish voters and politicians view snus, nicotine pouches and EU tobacco policy, and where parties risk falling out of step with their own voters ahead of the election.
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden has the EU's lowest proportion of smokers, with snus and nicotine pouches as alternatives to cigarettes. Meanwhile, the EU is pursuing a more restrictive approach, including proposed tax increases. Several member states, such as France, are banning white snus. The issue concerns not only public health but also representation, connection with voters and Sweden's freedom to act.

Two new Demoskop surveys compare public and political attitudes to tobacco, nicotine pouches and EU tobacco policy. The findings reveal where party positions align with public opinion and where clear gaps exist between voters and representatives.

EU decisions directly affect Swedish users because Sweden's snus exemption covers tobacco snus, not nicotine pouches.

The election determines Sweden's EU position. Which parties have their voters' support? Which risk falling out of step? Could nicotine policy affect party choice in September? After the presentation, contributors from politics, public opinion and public health comment on the findings.
content.subject: EU

content.description: A survey of Swedish companies shows that half have reduced investment in the sustainability transition over the past three years. Nine out of ten companies feel that the rules are unstable. What happens when companies doubt the long-term conditions?

content.title: Is Sweden wasting its competitiveness through inadequate gender equality?
content.description: Sweden is one of the world's most gender-equal countries, but men still form a clear majority on corporate boards. The research is clear: gender-equal organisations are more profitable and resilient. The question is not whether gender equality matters, but why it is still not a priority.
content.extendedDescription: Sweden has long been at the forefront of gender equality, yet progress on boards and in pay is slow. Why is gender equality still treated as a side issue? For many employers, efforts stop at good intentions because they lack tools for working systematically. But good intentions are not enough. On behalf of the government, Jämställdhetsmyndigheten, Statskontoret and Svenska institutet för standarder will work towards a European standard for effective gender equality work. This would give European organisations a concrete tool to manage and follow up their work properly, as a business-critical activity rather than a side project. The seminar brings together research, politics and business to explore what is needed for gender equality to become a competitive factor, rather than solely a matter of values.

content.title: How free is freedom of school choice really?
content.description: Pupils in adapted schools have a substantial need for appropriate support and adaptations, and the ability to choose a school is often crucial to their development. In practice, however, free choice does not apply: municipalities can circumvent it by offering insurance only in municipal schools or denying school transport despite rights under LSS.
content.extendedDescription:
Freedom of school choice is a statutory right, but for pupils with major and extensive support needs it is too often an illusion. A lack of transparency and widespread ignorance of these pupils' rights severely restrict that freedom. Loopholes exist and are exploited.

We are holding a seminar with a background presentation and overview of the evidence, featuring the headteacher/head of schools and the founder of the adapted school Move & Walk. The introduction highlights areas where pupils with major and extensive support needs are systematically disadvantaged.

This is followed by a political discussion with representatives of Centern and Moderaterna.

content.title: Does Sweden need anti-personnel mines?
content.description: Following the war in Ukraine, Sweden is again debating its ban on anti-personnel mines. Military benefits are weighed against humanitarian and environmental consequences. How should Sweden balance defence needs with international law and humanitarian commitments?
content.extendedDescription: This panel takes as its starting point the current Swedish debate on a possible withdrawal from the Ottawa Treaty and the reintroduction of anti-personnel mines. The debate brings together humanitarian, military, and legal perspectives, and asks how Sweden should assess the potential benefits and risks of such a policy shift. The panel will discuss what research and operational experience from past and current conflicts can tell us about the military utility of anti-personnel mines, their humanitarian consequences, and the legal implications of changing Sweden’s current position. The aim is to support a more evidence-based security policy debate. The key question is not only whether Sweden can use anti-personnel mines, but whether they would strengthen Swedish security enough to justify the documented risks for civilians, land use, infrastructure, and long-term recovery after war.
content.subject: Security/defence

content.title: From steel and paper to algorithms: Dalarna leads the way for Sweden's AI strategy
content.description: Sweden aims to become one of the world's ten leading AI nations. Billions are now being invested in data centres, AI infrastructure and a growing AI ecosystem in Dalarna. Could Dalarna be where Sweden's AI strategy turns from words into reality? What is needed, and who takes responsibility?
content.extendedDescription:
Dalarna is Sweden's next growth region and its new AI workshop. A strong industrial base, an exploratory public sector and rapidly growing AI infrastructure, including a European AI supercomputer, come together here. They create a unique environment where Sweden's AI strategy can move from paper to real action.

What role can a concerted regional effort play in Sweden's AI competitiveness? And how can a national strategy become tangible development in Dalarna here and now?

The seminar brings together decision-makers from politics, business and academia to discuss how AI initiatives can move from pilot to production and from vision to implementation. What must central government, regions and business do to succeed in Dalarna and Sweden? And how do we ensure that AI investment creates growth across the country?

content.title: How can Sweden's climate transition be fair and supported by the public?
content.description: How can the climate transition be both fast and fair – and win broad public support? Can reform proposals from researchers and civil society achieve the climate targets in a socially sustainable way, grounded in science?
content.extendedDescription:
How can Sweden transition to meet its climate targets with broad public support? Join a seminar about the report “Förslag för en folklig klimatpolitik”, where researchers and civil society present 24 reforms for a rapid, fair climate transition with public backing.

The seminar discusses how climate policy can reduce emissions while strengthening jobs, welfare and security. The discussion starts from the need to combine the climate transition with social justice. What is needed for more people to feel that the transition is possible, fair and worth taking part in?

The reform proposals were developed through interdisciplinary cooperation in the Fairtrans research programme. Their presentation is followed by panel discussions with organisations involved in Fairtrans and politicians.

The seminar is part of Uppsala universitet's climate days.

content.title: Sustainability risks in theory – business decisions in practice: how do we bridge the gap?
content.description: How can we make real progress on sustainability as demands for climate risk assessments, impact assessments and transition plans increase – while finance teams are expected to use the results in investment and strategic decisions?

This means moving from fragmented, manual data collection to integrated, standardised and quality-assured data management. But how do we get there?

Join Aspia's roundtable in Almedalen, where we bring together sustainability, finance and strategy teams to discuss:

- The challenges we face in strengthening the flow between sustainability-related and financial information.
- The role, opportunities and challenges of supporting systems.
- What is needed for a supporting system to generate the value an organisation wants.

The starting point is real experience of using supporting systems to advance organisations' sustainability work.

Format: Roundtable discussion.

Purpose: Identify shared challenges and concrete ways forward.

content.title: The Baltic Sea as a frontier zone and energy sea – a common strategy is needed!
content.description: Europe is facing two major challenges at the same time – a security crisis and a climate crisis. The Baltic Sea is in the middle of this, where large-scale energy production and security aspects must coexist. The need for a common strategy is obvious. How can Europe best deal with the situation now?
content.extendedDescription:
Major energy investments are planned by all democratic countries around the Baltic Sea. It is an important part of Europe's energy transition. This mainly concerns plans for offshore wind power and hydrogen. At the same time, the Baltic Sea is in the most vulnerable security situation since the end of the Second World War. How can these two great needs work together? How do Wind Europe view this? How do we achieve a common strategy for the development of the Baltic Sea that safeguards both these interests? 
The decisions have been made to make Bornholm the world's first energy island. Can more islands in the Baltic Sea follow, what can we learn from Bornholm? Estonia is planning for large wind farms near Gotland, how does that fit into the picture? We provide an overview of energy trends and security developments in the Baltic Sea.

content.title: A new approach lifts Rosengård – how housing companies can strengthen disadvantaged areas
content.description: A focus on residents' influence and maintaining order has increased safety, satisfaction and pride in Rosengård, Malmö. Two years after a new approach was introduced in Rosengård, clear results are visible and have also been confirmed by a research study.
content.extendedDescription:
The approach introduced by municipal housing company MKB combines three elements: preventive support, maintaining order and improved property management. It was designed following interviews with around 700 MKB tenants in Rosengård. Their wishes were clear: more preventive measures for children and young people, and a stronger focus on order, with consequences for misconduct.

After two years, researchers Peter Esaiasson and Jacob Sohlberg at Göteborgs universitet conducted follow-up interviews showing substantial positive changes and strong support among Rosengård residents for the approach. MKB's own customer surveys point in the same direction: for example, the proportion who would recommend their neighbourhood has increased markedly.

At the seminar, MKB and the researchers from Göteborgs universitet will jointly discuss:
- How a clear focus on residents' influence has improved the area.
- Examples of stronger collective capacity.
- How responsible behaviour has become the norm in recycling buildings and shared spaces.

content.title: Green competitiveness: making Sweden a leader in sustainable life science innovation
content.description: Sweden needs to turn sustainable pharmaceutical and medtech innovation into a competitive advantage. Stronger competitiveness requires clear incentives and simpler rules that stimulate research, development and early introduction of sustainable solutions.
content.extendedDescription: Environmentally sustainable innovation in pharmaceuticals and medical technology must shift from being seen as a costly requirement to becoming a competitive advantage. Countries investing in the climate transition become more attractive for future jobs and investment. For Sweden to lead, policies and regulations must create clear incentives for companies to invest in research, development and sustainable products, and to see Sweden as an attractive location for development, clinical trials and early introduction. Sustainable solutions require investment throughout their life cycle. Several initiatives already exist but see limited use. Standards such as PAS2090, which measures environmental impact at product level, can provide practical support. However, today's pharmaceutical substitution system does not consider sustainability. For companies to choose Sweden as an innovation environment, long-term, attractive conditions are needed to stimulate development of tomorrow's sustainable pharmaceuticals and medical technology.

content.title: More treatment options – a prerequisite for personalised care and investment in life science
content.description: Just over 30% of primary care doctors prescribe a different medicine each week from the one they consider most suitable, because of prescribing controls. More treatment options can enable more personalised asthma and COPD care. What risks arise from restricted treatment choices, and what is the impact on life science?
content.extendedDescription: A recent market survey of 893 primary care doctors shows that most view recommended medicine lists as helpful. However, just over 30% report prescribing a different medicine each week from the one they consider most appropriate, because of prescribing controls. Recommended lists must ensure patients with asthma and COPD have access to several treatment options and therefore more personalised care and well-controlled disease. Join a seminar where patients, experts and decision-makers discuss the risk of Sweden entering a monopoly-like situation if regions do not actively prioritise diversity in treatment options. Such a development would not only restrict patients' choices and affect care quality, but also reduce life science companies' willingness to invest and conduct research here, potentially weakening Sweden's position as a leading innovation nation over time.

content.title: What is needed to build new nuclear power in Sweden?
content.description: Several European countries are now investing in new nuclear power to meet energy needs and climate targets. Experience from previous reactor projects also shows that the approach taken is crucial to how efficiently expansion can be achieved. What is needed to build new nuclear power efficiently in Sweden?
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar focuses on the practical and industrial conditions for new nuclear power. In the first half, researchers from Uppsala universitet and the ANItA competence centre present new research on international experience of nuclear power expansion, new reactor technologies, global supply chains and possible sites for future reactors in Sweden. content.title: Hydrogen's role for Sweden: industry, the energy system and security of supply
content.description: Hydrogen is less about technology and more about what kind of Sweden we want to be. At a time of growing import dependence, global competition and energy transition, fossil-free hydrogen can strengthen competitiveness, security of supply and the climate transition where alternatives are lacking. What role should it play?
content.extendedDescription:
Please note that the entire hydrogen arena is broadcast via the link above.

In this seminar, we show how and in what form hydrogen can contribute to a more competitive Sweden that is independent of fossil fuels. Topics include hydrogen's role in the energy system, from local initiatives to national development. What role does hydrogen play in the energy system of the future? What synergies are there with district heating? And how can hydrogen contribute to greater flexibility, security of supply and resilience in the electricity system, both locally and nationally? We bring together industry stakeholders and researchers to discuss how hydrogen creates value, from municipal initiatives to large-scale investments. Through concrete examples, we highlight how hydrogen connects electricity, industry and transport, and what is needed for more participants to help realise its potential.

content.title: Why should we protect children?
content.description: Increasingly young children are being recruited into criminal acts and serious violent offences. content.extendedDescription: The discussion centres on young people's vulnerability. Meet researchers and practitioners discussing society's preventive work to create safe settings and counter exclusion, youth crime and recruitment into gangs. We ask researchers at Svenska Kriminalpolitiska laboratoriet about the effects of policy reforms, and researchers and practitioners how knowledge of successful collaboration and intervention models can be shared and used more widely. During the seminar, we will also consider the risks when researchers and practitioners feel political decisions conflict with science and proven experience. How do we promote safer environments for children and young people as part of crime prevention and enforcement? content.title: How can we help more young people get their first job?
content.description: Many young people want to work, while employers report difficulty finding the right skills. Yet they fail to connect. Why is this, and what needs to change so that more young people can enter working life?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden has high youth unemployment compared with many other European countries. At the same time, employers in several sectors report skills shortages and difficulty finding the right staff. This points to a clear gap between young people and the labour market.
What causes it? Is it education, employers' requirements or the way systems are designed? And what is needed for more young people to actually get a chance at their first job?
The business community has recently launched a joint initiative to help excluded young people into work, aiming to get 100 000 young people into jobs through 1 000 companies over the next ten years. But what conditions are needed for more employers to recruit? What role does politics play — and what responsibility does business have?

In this discussion, representatives of political youth organisations come together to discuss practical solutions for lowering barriers to the labour market.

content.title: Climate targets meet public responsibilities
content.description: How can Sweden build safer and more sustainable public-service buildings? Timber-based building systems for remand centres, prisons and barracks. Timber offers flexible, scalable solutions with a low climate impact, faster processes and maintained security. What is the way forward?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden needs to expand public-service buildings such as remand centres, prisons and barracks. At the same time, climate targets and the security situation, not least the war in Ukraine, demand faster, smarter and more resilient construction. The seminar explores how timber-based building systems can contribute.

We highlight innovation, client requirements and how public-sector organisations can drive progress with climate-smart and flexible solutions. We discuss the needs of total defence and the role of industry, as well as how timber can strengthen preparedness through shorter lead times and domestic production.

The discussion covers carbon storage, prefabrication, circularity and flexible use. We analyse the capacity of the timber value chain and what is needed to scale up. Fire issues are also addressed, with a focus on safety, durability and modern solutions.

Together, we discuss how Sweden can develop robust and climate-smart public-service buildings in timber.
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: How can Sweden secure industrial investment worth billions and jobs amid global competition?
content.description: What does Sweden need to win more investment? Sweden has global leadership in industrial innovation to defend and strengthen. content.extendedDescription:
Join this moderated panel discussion in Business Sweden's garden, where we explore how international companies' operations contribute to Swedish prosperity and examine global competition.

They strengthen Swedish value chains, drive research and innovation, provide capital and build Sweden's long-term competitiveness. Sweden's appeal rests on genuine strengths in stability, predictability and technological leadership, but competition from countries actively removing barriers is intensifying.

Companies evaluating Sweden encounter challenges with energy availability, permitting, skills supply and incentives. Encouraging existing operations to expand and stay is as important as attracting new ones.

content.title: Swedish migration policy today and tomorrow — legally secure and sustainable choices
content.description: Swedish asylum and migration policy is currently undergoing extensive changes. The reforms affect many people and have long-term consequences. How can we shape sustainable migration policy for the future?
content.extendedDescription:
Swedish asylum and migration policy is currently undergoing extensive changes. National reforms and the implementation of the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum mean far-reaching changes to both rules and practice. These decisions will have long-term consequences for legal certainty, integration, sustainable return and Sweden's role in European and global cooperation.
The discussion will address what returning people to crisis-affected countries entails. What role does resettlement play in receiving refugees? What is at stake if the European Convention on Human Rights is reinterpreted, and how is legal certainty affected by so-called ‘safe third countries’ and return hubs?
Act Svenska kyrkan and RESCUE invite you to a discussion with the parties' migration policy spokespersons about legally secure and sustainable choices for the migration policy of the future.

content.title: When election promises must become action
content.description: Opinion polls come thick and fast in election years. Parties do what they can to influence public opinion. What do we know about election promises' influence on opinion and campaigns – do they matter? What will happen to promises made in the 2026 campaign? Politics has recently become both more engaging and more polarising. Seminar participants discuss how to turn visions into reality and exert influence in practice, and how political reforms should be designed and implemented to become reality.

content.title: How can the public sector strengthen its procurement capability for the future?
content.description: Public procurement must contribute to sustainability, preparedness and secure supplies while demands for commercial competence increase. How can the public sector strengthen its skills and capability to meet new societal challenges?
content.extendedDescription:
Public procurement exceeds SEK 1000 billion each year and affects everything from the climate transition and welfare to preparedness, security of supply and efforts to combat welfare fraud. In a more uncertain world, the procurement function has taken on an increasingly strategic role, while demands relating to law, sustainability, commercial competence, digitalisation and AI are rising rapidly.

How can the public sector ensure it has the right skills to meet these demands? Drawing on SOI's updated competency profile, we discuss the skills and ways of working needed to strengthen the profession, improve delivery quality and create public-sector business relationships that are sustainable over the long term.

The discussion brings perspectives on governance, sustainability, preparedness and practical implementation, focusing on how central government, regions and municipalities can equip their organisations for future challenges.

content.title: Is solidarity dead?
content.description: Aid budgets are shrinking and global health programmes are closing. Sweden debates who is entitled to care. Is solidarity retreating, or already dead? What is at stake when the world chooses to look away?
content.extendedDescription:
Something is changing in how we speak about and take responsibility for one another. Nationalism is gaining ground. Aid is dismissed as naive.
Countries that once led global health efforts are withdrawing, with consequences measured in closed clinics, interrupted vaccination programmes and lives not saved. We see this now in eastern Congo: an ongoing Ebola outbreak where health workers previously funded by USAID are no longer present and coordination has collapsed.
It is not only the USA. The UK, Germany and Canada are cutting back. Sweden is reducing aid and has phased out development cooperation with several countries.
Sweden's domestic debate is also affected. It is therefore relevant to ask where solidarity's boundaries lie, including in healthcare. This ethics discussion brings together different perspectives. Join us in seeking answers.
What does shrinking solidarity cost? And what are we prepared to do about it?

content.title: An ADHD diagnosis: desirable to get – and to get rid of?
content.description: Sweden has one of the world's highest proportions of ADHD diagnoses. A new market is emerging for people who want their diagnosis removed. Who is responsible for removing diagnoses? Are all diagnoses needed, or should society's support systems be organised differently?
content.extendedDescription:
The number of ADHD diagnoses has multiplied over two decades. We now see the next phase: a growing group seeking reassessment of their diagnosis, and a private market offering it for 9,000 to 30,000 kronor.
An ADHD diagnosis opens doors to support and treatment that make a real difference. But when it also closes doors to education and professions, lifelong consequences arise. Who is responsible when a diagnosis is no longer relevant or perhaps was wrong from the start: the person who made it, the system that created demand, or the individual who sought help? Is removing a diagnosis a task for public healthcare? How should reassessment be prioritised relative to other care? Is there a risk that demand rather than need drives healthcare?
Some also argue that healthcare and other sectors should focus on abilities and needs rather than diagnoses. How would such a shift work? Who would gain and who would lose?

content.title: Smart pills – care or control?
content.description: Tomorrow's pills could confirm that you have taken your medicine – and notify healthcare providers. Support for self-care when every dose counts. But the same technology could become surveillance. Where is the boundary?
content.extendedDescription:
In January 2026, researchers published a study of a new digital pill. It is not the first of its kind, but it solves a problem with earlier versions: existing smart pills contain non-degradable components that must pass through the body intact, risking harm to the patient with long-term use. The new pill contains components that largely dissolve in the stomach. Only a small chip passes through.
Many patients with chronic illnesses do not take their medicines as prescribed. Smart pills reduce the risk of missed medication for people for whom every missed dose could have serious consequences. But the technology raises ethical questions: who should own data about whether we take our medicines? Is there a risk that smart pills will be disproportionately targeted at vulnerable groups? And if the technology becomes safe and available to everyone, should it become standard in all future medicines? Who decides where helping a patient ends and monitoring a citizen begins?

content.title: Robots, social contact and divorce — conditions and solutions for tomorrow's eldercare
content.description: What kind of later life is possible and desirable at a time when the proportion of older people is growing faster than ever?
content.extendedDescription:
Together with seven organisations in eldercare, we have explored the conditions for later life tomorrow — a life that a rapidly growing share of Swedes should be able to live with dignity, despite acute skills shortages in many welfare professions.

More than 1000 Swedes born in 1945-1954, along with hundreds of relatives and care staff, have answered questions such as:

• What do today's 70-80-year-olds consider the most desirable ways to address the challenges of an ageing population?
• Who is most concerned about older people's perceived loneliness, and how does social contact actually develop after retirement?
• How can older people be encouraged to leave their sought-after homes and move to housing better suited to their long-term needs?
• What potential for automation exists in eldercare, and what do older people themselves think of the technological solutions?

Insights and observations are discussed with a panel comprising:
Daniel Hansson, Head of Health Promotion for Older People in Österåkers kommun.
Marcus Fält, Head of the Care Homes Segment, Attendo

content.title: Public health, freedom or bans? The future of nicotine in the EU
content.description: In Sweden, smoking has been replaced by snus and nicotine pouches. The EU's review of the Tobacco Products Directive could now change the conditions. Are the new nicotine products a public health problem or part of the solution – and what position will Sweden take after the 2026 election?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden has reached the smoke-free target (fewer than five per cent smokers). Snus and nicotine pouches have played, and continue to play, a central role in Sweden's success. The EU's review of the Tobacco Products Directive could affect Sweden's ability to pursue its own nicotine policy in the future. The new products are not covered by the snus exemption. What does this mean for everyone who has stopped smoking using nicotine pouches? How will Sweden respond to new EU proposals restricting or banning new nicotine products?
Party representatives will be questioned about their positions ahead of the forthcoming EU negotiations.
How do the parties view the fundamental conflict between
- a policy of continuing to reduce smoking, in which substitute products play an important role, and
- a policy of reducing all nicotine use, meaning restricted access to substitute products?
The seminar opens with a short background on the processes surrounding the Tax Directive and Tobacco Products Directive currently being decided in the EU, and what is at stake for Sweden.
content.subject: EU
speakerTitles: Spokesperson on Social Affairs and LGBTQIA Issues
Chair of the Committee on Industry and Trade

content.title: From law to reality: why is nicotine reaching minors?
content.description: Despite clear legislation, minors can widely obtain nicotine products. Use among young people is increasing and, in many cases, the products are far too easy to obtain. Supervisory responsibility is divided between several levels, but outcomes point to significant shortcomings in compliance and oversight.
content.extendedDescription: How can it be so easy for minors to obtain nicotine despite legal requirements and supervision? The seminar presents a new survey of municipalities' test purchases, showing how the rules work in practice. We examine the chain of responsibility from legislation to local supervision and hear how key players view the issue: retailers, industry organisations, municipalities, county administrative boards and Folkhälsomyndigheten. content.title: From gaps in the system to coordinated support: could a Mental Health Reform 2.0 be the way forward?
content.description: More people are seeking psychiatric care, but many do not receive help. What is needed to close the gaps between needs and services? How can we build a system that works for patients and the professionals supporting people in need?
content.extendedDescription:
Thirty years after the mental health reform, the visions of early intervention, coordinated care and secure lives remain far from fulfilled. As more children, young people and adults seek help, we see fewer inpatient beds and inadequate cooperation between psychiatric services, municipalities and emergency services. Healthcare staff, police and rescue services encounter the consequences every day: people in acute distress and a fragmented system.

The seminar brings together patient representatives, experts and politicians to discuss what is needed for functioning psychiatric care. How can we ensure early intervention for children and young people? How do we strengthen support for adults with complex needs? Which political priorities are required to build a lasting system in which more people actually have the opportunity to feel better?

Join a seminar highlighting gaps in the system and opportunities to reconnect society's safety net.

content.title: The pocketbook election of 2026 – what do voters want from economic policy?
content.description: Sweden is approaching another election in which the economy and household finances are expected to take centre stage. What do voters really want: measures that improve their own finances here and now, or reforms that strengthen Sweden's economy over the long term?
content.extendedDescription:
Join a discussion about economic policy ahead of the 2026 election: the reforms implemented, how voters have received them and the choices ahead.

The discussion starts from a new survey by Länsförsäkringar and Verian on how Swedish households view some of this parliamentary term's major economic reforms. These include tax cuts on work and pensions, reduced food VAT, lower electricity and fuel costs, tax-free ISK savings and new mortgage rules.

The survey shows how the reforms are assessed generally, for personal finances and for Sweden's economy. This raises a central question for the seminar: is it enough for policies to be felt in household budgets, or must they also be seen as credible for Sweden in the long term?

content.title: Is now the time to end homelessness?
content.description:
So far, efforts to tackle homelessness have been small, fragmented and insufficient. But there is now momentum to end homelessness:
• A new national homelessness strategy creates new opportunities
• A new Social Services Act focuses on prevention
• A new EU plan for affordable housing
content.extendedDescription:
Homelessness is not only a social problem. It is also about ensuring enough homes for people with different financial circumstances. To solve the persistent housing problem, social and housing policy must work together, and politicians, public authorities and property owners need new ways to cooperate.

During this seminar, the panel will discuss:
How can decision-makers take responsibility for ensuring that the homelessness strategy and Social Services Act work together so that everyone experiencing homelessness gets a home?

How can decision-makers, property owners and civil society cooperate to provide more affordable housing so everyone can afford a home?

And especially: how do we seize this unique opportunity and move from words to action to end homelessness?

content.title: From property financing to financing society – does our view of investment need to change?
content.description: Sweden has substantial investment needs, while financing conditions have become more challenging. Risk now encompasses not only economics, but also climate, energy and social sustainability. Meeting these challenges requires new rules and business models that reward sustainable value creation.
content.extendedDescription:
The low interest rates and abundant capital of recent decades have been replaced by higher capital costs, geopolitical uncertainties, increased sustainability requirements and growing investment needs. Sweden needs to develop cities, modernise infrastructure and energy systems, and adapt its existing property stock to climate change. The question is not whether these investments are needed, but how they will be financed and who is prepared to invest.

How should investors, banks and property owners value investments whose societal benefits are clear but whose financial returns materialise only over a long period? Meeting these challenges requires stable long-term rules, new business models and forms of investment that reward partnerships and sustainable value creation.

content.title: Today's healthcare, tomorrow's solutions – greater national and regional collaboration for innovation
content.description: How do we secure the healthcare of the future when needs are growing faster than resources? Innovation is crucial to saving lives, strengthening the quality of care and creating sustainable societies. Yet today, many solutions get stuck in pilot projects. What is needed nationally for innovation to deliver real benefits for patients?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden is a world leader in research and innovation, but considerably less successful at implementing new solutions at scale. Innovations get stuck in pilot projects, health data is difficult to use, clinical trials take too long and patients' access to new treatments varies depending on where they live.

The seminar brings together leading representatives of national and regional politics, healthcare, patient organisations and business to discuss how Sweden can create better conditions for innovation in healthcare, and why this is crucial to future patient benefit, quality of care and competitiveness.

content.title: Threats and violence against essential workers – who takes responsibility?
content.description: Ambulance staff and others on the front line increasingly face threats and violence. What is needed to ensure a safe working environment without compromising rapid help for those who need it?
content.extendedDescription:
When an ambulance service employee lost their life on duty, a difficult but necessary question came into focus: how safe are those tasked with helping others in vulnerable and unpredictable situations?

What happened was not an isolated incident. The investigation shows that something similar could have happened elsewhere. Ambulance staff, healthcare workers and other public employees face threats and violence at work. Many work alone or in small teams, in people's homes, in public places and in situations where risks can change rapidly.

At the same time, their mission is clear: help must arrive quickly when people need it. But is responsibility for employees' safety equally clear?

The seminar addresses the tension between rapid, accessible help and employers' responsibility for a safe working environment. What can be resolved locally, and what requires national decisions?

content.title: Is healthcare best run as a company? Sweden's most talked-about primary care reform
content.description: Gävleborg is the first in the country to turn publicly operated primary care into a company. What was the result, and what does it mean for the rest of Sweden?
content.extendedDescription:
Swedish primary care is under severe pressure. Access, working conditions and patient safety are recurring challenges. Meanwhile, there is widespread discussion about how care should be governed and organised to meet future needs.

Region Gävleborg has chosen a new path. In one year, 25 health centres and 850 employees moved from public administration into a region-owned company. This is the first time a Swedish region has implemented such a change within its own operations.

The decision has prompted strong reactions. Some see a bold approach to improving conditions for primary care. Others see a risky experiment in an already strained part of healthcare.

What can other regions learn from Gävleborg's choice? Has Region Gävleborg found a new path, or does the change show that primary care cannot develop on its own?

content.title: Glaucoma care in transition – those who live should be able to see
content.description: Glaucoma is a common disease affecting hundreds of thousands of patients and is the leading cause of irreversible blindness. For patients, this means a dramatic decline in quality of life, while the burden and costs for healthcare keep increasing. New treatment methods can prevent this!
content.extendedDescription: In an educational seminar, we will hear both the glaucoma surgeon's and the patient's perspectives, and explore the opportunities offered by fully implementing medical technology and benefiting from its positive effects. In this case, that means not only reducing the risk of patients with glaucoma becoming visually impaired or even blind, but also easing pressure on healthcare and substantially reducing the costs of glaucoma care overall. In a chronic disease where patients cannot regain lost sight, all attempts to halt or delay progression are clearly beneficial. Not least because quality of life is enormously affected for the unfortunate patients who become severely ill, often unnecessarily. We also know that a very large share of the burden and costs falls on these severely ill patients. We therefore cannot afford NOT to treat patients earlier – and patients, surgeons, health economists and healthcare representatives agree on this.
content.detail: VOLARE – in cooperation with SWEDISH MEDTECH, the medical technology industry association

content.title: How will the circular society be financed?
content.description: The transition to a more circular society, where resources are used more efficiently in circular flows, can help reduce our environmental and climate impact, lower business risks such as resource shortages and price volatility, and create value through benefits such as increased productivity.
content.extendedDescription:
This transition will bring major changes in how we live and consume, and drive substantial changes in companies' business models. One example is moving from selling capital-intensive products to charging for the function or benefit they provide: product-as-a-service. What does the transition to a circular economy mean for households and businesses? How will it be financed? What role can banks and sustainable financing solutions play?

Join a conversation about drivers, challenges and opportunities, and above all the paths and partnerships needed to make the transition to a more circular society succeed.

content.title: Nobelbanan + Mälarbanan = a perfect match?
content.description: Can a regional route-location study accelerate Sweden's most profitable railway project?
content.extendedDescription:
Is Nobelbanan from Örebro to Karlstad, connecting to Oslo, the next step in Mälarbanan's development? Is Mälarbanan ready for a new national role, and can the regions help develop national planning?

When Mälarbanan was built in the late 1990s, it was Sweden's first major railway investment in many years. It launched the development of regional rail travel in Sweden. The route-location study for Nobelbanan is now nearing completion. Extending Mälarbanan with Nobelbanan is the next step both in expanding functional regions and in building a strong Nordic region.

In 2024, the regions along the Oslo-Stockholm corridor and Trafikverket decided to launch a pilot project involving a route-location study for Nobelbanan. What can we learn from a regionally led route-location study? Can it provide better input for national planning and enable a faster planning process?

content.title: Sweden wastes the potential of 5 000 young people with neurodevelopmental conditions in every age cohort — can business afford to stand by?
content.description: While employers talk about skills shortages, thousands of young people with neurodevelopmental conditions lack effective routes into work. How do we build workplaces that can serve as a first step into working life, and what do employers need to dare to open the door?
content.extendedDescription:
Today, substantial resources go into adapting individuals to working life, but far less into developing workplaces that work for people with different ways of functioning. As a result, employers who see potential still hesitate, while young people get stuck between different systems.
A business sector that works only for some will also struggle to build the skills and resilience the future requires.
What do employers need to move from willingness to action?
Could a traineeship programme for young people with neurodevelopmental conditions — focusing as much on workplace development as on the individual — be part of the solution?
A few brief perspectives open the discussion. After that, the experiences and ideas in the room are as important as those shared from the stage.
content.subject: Business

content.title: How can we continue successfully combating financial crime?
content.description: In recent years, society has taken decisive measures against organised and financial crime, with results. However, major challenges remain, and further action across society is needed to continue curbing crime.
content.extendedDescription:
Measures taken by politicians, police, banks and other authorities in recent years against organised and financial crime, including legislative changes, increased resources, stronger cooperation and new security solutions, have had positive effects. For example, profits from telephone fraud have fallen substantially and shootings have decreased sharply. Yet the criminal economy continues to grow. A report from Expertgruppen för studier i offentlig ekonomi concluded early this year that the criminal economy turns over 352 billion kronor annually.

How can we best continue countering organised and financial crime and the criminal economy? What additional measures are needed, and in which areas? How can banks contribute further? How can practical cooperation and information sharing between authorities and business become even more effective?

content.title: How do we restore trust when fake is the new normal?
content.description:
Source criticism is being challenged now that false content is often impossible to detect with the naked eye. When technology makes truth difficult to establish, the problem shifts from information to trust: whom can we trust, and why?
At the same time, trust risks replacing critical thinking.
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar starts from a shift in how we view source criticism: from exposing false content to understanding sources, intentions and trust. Drawing on Arbetets museum's “Demokratilabbet”, stakeholders from the social partners, culture and defence – together forming the country's most credible voice – come together to discuss how to strengthen resilience against disinformation in practice.
The conversation highlights different perspectives on the threats, the changing role of trust and what it takes to build and maintain credibility. The focus is on solutions: how organisations can jointly contribute to open discussion, critical thinking and a more resilient democracy, particularly in workplaces where many people meet every day.

content.title: The road to a resilient and competitive electricity system — how do we get there?
content.description: Electrification, geopolitical tensions and volatile electricity prices are increasing the demands on Sweden's electricity system. How do we build a system that can withstand crises, enable investment and deliver fossil-free electricity at competitive prices?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's electricity system needs to become both more resilient and more competitive. It must withstand disruptions and crises, adapt to changing conditions and recover quickly after outages or strains. At the same time, it needs to deliver fossil-free electricity with high reliability, stable prices and predictable investment conditions.

Achieving this requires flexibility in generation, storage and demand, diversified electricity production and robust grid infrastructure with redundancy and reserve capacity. Equally important are available grid capacity, efficient permitting processes and long-term political ground rules that enable profitable investment. How can Sweden build an electricity system that both withstands disruptions and strengthens competitiveness?

content.title: Beyond age limits: protecting and supporting children online, where they are
content.description: Following the government inquiry into age limits for social media, what does this mean in practice for children and young people? And how do we move from regulation to real safety in their digital lives?
content.extendedDescription:
Children encounter both risks and opportunities online. They may face harmful content and grooming, but also find community, support and knowledge. Meanwhile, many young people describe a growing divide from the adult world, and we see them increasingly turning to AI for advice and support on sensitive issues.

UNICEF Sverige and Spotify bring together stakeholders from politics, civil society and business to discuss:
- How digital platforms must take responsibility for children's safety and wellbeing regardless of age limits.
- How society needs to reach young people and offer support where they are.
- How we bridge understanding across ages and generations and strengthen young people's resilience as AI becomes more important.

content.title: The right to asylum and Swedish asylum policy – are they compatible?
content.description: Sweden has adopted many national asylum laws in recent years while the EU's new Pact on Migration and Asylum is being implemented. But how well do the new laws respect international law, particularly the right to asylum?
content.extendedDescription:
In just a few years, Swedish asylum policy has been reformed in line with a political desire to sharply reduce immigration to Sweden. Some effects have received more attention than others, such as the deportation of teenagers, babies and very elderly people living alone. Is this policy compatible with the right to asylum? content.title: Cooperation is not enough: how do we make research make a difference?
content.description: There is no shortage of research, innovations or technological solutions. But why do promising initiatives often stop at pilots, despite major needs and available solutions?
content.extendedDescription:
Research should contribute to innovation and public value through interaction with the public sector, business and civil society. Yet many initiatives end as projects. Making them a reality requires shared responsibility and the courage to invest for the long term.
We often see this in prevention and societal transition: research identifies interventions with long-term effects, but costs arise here and now while benefits may accrue to other actors later. A gap then emerges between knowledge and action: projects are carried out, but implementation does not follow. Everyone sees the need, but no one drives change all the way. Can change be achieved, and if so, how?
The problem is rarely a lack of knowledge, ideas or willingness, but how we organise, finance and take responsibility for change. We discuss how a solution becomes usable, by whom and on what terms, guided by three questions: who receives the value, who pays and who must change how they work?
content.subject: Research

content.title: From projects to outcomes – can outcomes-based contracts scale up prevention?
content.description: Sweden faces increasing ill health and growing welfare costs. Despite strong evidence for prevention, scaling up preventive measures is difficult. How can new governance and funding models create better conditions for long-term investment in health?
content.extendedDescription:
Despite strong evidence for prevention, Sweden struggles to move from pilot projects and temporary initiatives to long-term investment at scale. One important explanation is that today's governance and funding models often reward activities rather than achieved outcomes.
Outcomes-based contracts are attracting growing interest. By linking payments to verified outcomes, public, private and non-profit organisations can create new incentives for prevention. But which societal challenges are suited to outcomes-based funding? How can outcomes be measured credibly? And what changes are needed for prevention to become an investment rather than a cost?
Anders Ekholm from Ett Friskare Sverige opens the seminar and then moderates a discussion on how Sweden can take the next step, from projects to outcomes and from short-term interventions to long-term investment in health.
The event is part of Life Science-dagen, an initiative by Medicon Village.
content.subject: Health and social care

content.title: Many of us stand behind the call – Russia out of Ukraine!
content.description: More than four years ago, on 24 February 2022, Russia launched a full-scale invasion of neighbouring Ukraine in violation of international law. content.extendedDescription:
We invite everyone to join a demonstration independent of political parties and organisations to show that Sweden stands behind Ukraine's struggle for freedom, peace and independence! Together with civil society organisations, we gather around a shared demand – Russia out of Ukraine!

For just over four years, Ukraine has endured an inhumane assault, with constant drone and missile attacks. The Ukrainian population faces continuous suffering and oppression. Meanwhile, the Ukrainian army is fighting heroically against an occupying power and has succeeded in stopping Russia's initial plan to occupy all of Ukraine.

Today, Ukraine's eastern border is not only a boundary with an aggressive neighbour, but a boundary between democratic Europe and imperialist Russia. Ukraine is fighting for a democratic Europe today. We must therefore give Ukraine all the support it needs in its struggle. For Ukraine! For Europe! And for Sweden! Slava Ukraini!

content.title: From action plan to reality: diagnostics as the connecting thread in cardiovascular health
content.description: Cardiovascular disease is our most widespread major disease. The government's remit for a new action plan emphasises prevention, early detection and equitable care. But success requires a clear link to healthcare. Is diagnostics the connecting thread needed to turn fine words into reality?
content.extendedDescription:
The answer is an unequivocal YES!

The action plan must not remain a paper exercise. The government emphasises prevention, early detection and equitable care, but one crucial word is missing: diagnostics. Since most care decisions start here, the field must be prioritised so that we can use its full potential to save lives and relieve pressure on healthcare.

We do not need to reinvent the wheel. Lessons from many years of investment in cancer care can help us get the direction right from the outset. We need to shift attention and resources from reactive treatment to proactive healthcare.

Join a solutions-focused discussion in Almedalen where we identify the way forward for stronger cardiovascular health. Early, equitable and innovative diagnostics is the engine that makes the vision of no premature deaths from cardiovascular disease a reality.

content.title: Sweden lacks safe rest areas for commercial transport – a systemic failure that threatens the entire transport chain
content.description:
Sweden's lorry drivers perform a critical societal function – without them, Sweden stops.
Yet there is a major shortage of secure lorry parking for commercial transport, both in Sweden and across Europe. The problem is not a lack of awareness, but a lack of responsibility, incentives and implementation.
content.extendedDescription:
Resilient transport infrastructure is crucial to Sweden's supply chain and preparedness. Despite broad agreement on the need for more and better rest areas, too little is happening. Responsibilities are unclear, incentives are weak and implementation stalls.
This seminar moves from describing the problem to addressing responsibility. We identify why progress has stalled and what is needed to produce concrete solutions.
We bring together actors from the entire chain: business, politics and people with first-hand experience from the road. Together, we discuss what a functioning model for future rest areas could look like, with clear responsibilities, relevant requirements and feasible solutions.

• What is preventing the expansion of safe rest areas in Sweden?
• How do today's shortcomings affect transport capacity and delivery reliability?
• What concrete requirements should be placed on the state, municipalities and business?
• What does it take to create a transport sector that can cope with both everyday conditions and crises?
• Are we willing to pay for social responsibility?

content.title: Leadership for working life in times of great uncertainty and rapid change
content.description: Working life is shaped by rapid change, AI, geopolitical shifts and economic pressure. When direction, focus and collaboration falter, organisations lose momentum. The question is how leaders can create clarity, trust and the ability to act without having all the answers.
content.extendedDescription:
The event takes the form of a guided breakfast walk from 08.00-08.50. We meet at Strandvägen 1, Kallis, where Siri Wikander from Beyond Talking welcomes participants, briefly introduces the survey and frames the discussion.

During the walk, we explore two questions: what leadership is needed when uncertainty and the pace of change are high, and how organisations can develop that capability in practice.

The walk ends where we started, with a short summary. The content is based on Beyond Talking's survey “Ledarskapsinsikter inför 2026”.
